graphics.question: How does a federal grant actually travel from Congress to a city, and what records prove each step?
graphics.answer: Congress sets the purpose and budget authority, OMB apportions it, HUD makes the prime awards (for FY2024 HOME: $23,907,179 to New York's Housing Trust Fund Corporation and $1,303,112.35 directly to the City of Syracuse), Treasury's Fiscal Service pays, and auditors test afterward. graphics.question: Where does the FY2027 budget request add or cut money, agency by agency?
graphics.answer: The April request raises estimated federal outlays from $7,540.4 billion to $8,092.9 billion. Measured in base discretionary budget authority, the biggest increases are Defense Department (+28%) and Justice (+13%); the deepest cuts are Small Business Administration (-70%), National Science Foundation (-55%), Environmental Protection Agency (-52%). A request is not law: FY2027 is running on a continuing resolution through December 11, 2026.

graphics.question: Which federal bodies are on the government's own books, and which sit outside?
graphics.answer: Of the 352 bodies on the federal tree (committees counted separately), 271 are counted in the government's own audited statements. 26 are disclosed but kept off the books (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Amtrak, The Federal Reserve System), 13 are related parties the U.S. influences but does not control (Federal Home Loan Banks, IMF, IBRD), and 33 sit outside (Farm Credit System, Brand USA, In-Q-Tel); 9 have no placement yet. The test is the federal accounting standard SFFAS 47. The 25 Reserve Bank branch offices are listed too and counted with their Reserve Bank; Buffalo is closed but stays listed.

graphics.question: Which advisory boards, research centers and councils belong to, or advise, which federal agency?

graphics.question: Who has a Federal Reserve account, and who is still waiting?
graphics.answer: No crypto firm is confirmed to hold a full Federal Reserve master account. Kraken has a limited-purpose account; Anchorage Digital is waiting for a decision; Custodia Bank is fighting its denial in court.

graphics.question: Master account, limited account or payment account: what is the difference?
graphics.answer: A master account gives full access to the Fed's payment services and its credit. A limited-purpose account (so far only Kraken's) gives payment access without the Fed's credit, and the proposed payment account would do something similar for a new class of firms. Without any account, a firm reaches the Fed only through a bank that has one.

graphics.question: Who has legal authority over each part of the U.S. securities and payments plumbing?
graphics.answer: No single body. The library maps 89 U.S. laws, agencies, market bodies and failure-handling roles, joined by 96 recorded legal links; 37 of them are the market institutions, accounts and settlement services themselves. The agencies with the most supervisory links into market institutions and settlement services are Securities and Exchange Commission (12), Commodity Futures Trading Commission (7) and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (5). The Financial Stability Oversight Council designated 8 utilities as systemically important (CLS Bank International, Chicago Mercantile Exchange, DTC, FICC, ICE Clear Credit, NSCC, Options Clearing Corporation and The Clearing House Payments Company); under Title VIII each has a supervisory agency: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System for The Clearing House Payments Company and CLS Bank International; Commodity Futures Trading Commission for Chicago Mercantile Exchange and ICE Clear Credit; Securities and Exchange Commission for DTC, NSCC, FICC and Options Clearing Corporation. DTC alone answers to 4: Financial Stability Oversight Council (designates), Securities and Exchange Commission (Title VIII supervisory agency), New York Department of Financial Services (state trust supervision) and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (state member bank supervision).

graphics.question: What do 'settled' and 'final' really mean for an ACH payment, a tokenized stock and a DTC token?
graphics.answer: They mean different things in each system, and "final" in one record does not settle the others. ACH: The Reserve Bank debits the sending bank and credits the receiving bank at the scheduled time. For a credit item, the receiving bank's settlement credit is final and available under Operating Circular 4. Securitize tokenized stock: The product is designed to exchange the CET and USDC atomically on Solana. Solana can make the token transfer technically confirmed while Securitize determines the governed entitlement state. DTC token: The entitlement representation moves between registered participant wallets free of value. DTC's official record recognizes the participant wallet location of the entitlement.

graphics.answer: Of the 12 market-infrastructure systems in the library, 1 is recorded as settling in central-bank money: the Sterling Fnality Payment System, run by Fnality UK Ltd (supervised by the Bank of England). 4 move banks' own tokenized deposits, which are commercial-bank money, and for the other 7 the library does not say what money they settle in.

graphics.question: When must U.S. Treasury trades be centrally cleared, and which clearinghouses can do it?
graphics.answer: Under the SEC rule adopted December 13, 2023, eligible secondary-market Treasury cash trades must be centrally cleared by December 31, 2026, and repo by June 30, 2027; the SEC said in February 2025 it does not intend further extensions. Three clearinghouses are registered to do it: FICC (DTCC's subsidiary, the incumbent), CME Securities Clearing (registered December 1, 2025; its launch moved from Q2 to 'later in 2026') and ICE Clear Credit (its Treasury business approved January 30, 2026). The mandate does not apply to the Fed's own operations; clearing those is still only a proposal.

graphics.question: Which Reserve Bank runs which national payment and Treasury service?
graphics.answer: The Fed's national services are spread across the twelve Reserve Banks, each a separate legal corporation. graphics.answer: So far the courts side with the Fed. Custodia has asked the Supreme Court to take the case, and the Fed opposed review on October 13, 2026.

graphics.question: Did the ban on 'reputation risk' debanking become law, and at which agencies?
graphics.answer: It became agency regulation, not a law passed by Congress: the OCC and FDIC adopted a final rule (April 10, 2026); the NCUA adopted a final rule (June 25, 2026); the Federal Reserve Board has only proposed one (February 26, 2026). The NCUA's rule says it implements Executive Order 14331 (signed August 7, 2025 · published August 12, 2025).

graphics.question: Who really owns your loan?
graphics.answer: Often not the bank or brand you see. In Affirm's program agreements filed with the SEC (November 2020), Cross River Bank is the named lender, Affirm buys most of the loans, owns the customer information and services them, and Upstart processes applications and keeps the register of who owns the note. On the library's July 11, 2026 reading, the Affirm Card is issued by Evolve or Stride, not Cross River, and Upstart's note permits sale without borrower consent and discloses the owner only on written request.

graphics.question: Has the federal government really stopped sending paper checks?
graphics.answer: Mostly, not entirely. Executive Order 14247 (signed March 25, 2025 · published March 28, 2025) ordered an end to paper checks for federal payments, and a customs notice of July 8, 2026 says the government no longer sends them; but the Treasury's own April 29, 2026 proposal still sets out when agencies may send one, and the PBGC was moving its remaining paper-check recipients on June 24, 2026. In FY2026 Treasury screened >1.1 billion payment requests (about $3.7 trillion) before the money went out.

graphics.question: How big is FedNow now, and how fast is it growing?
graphics.answer: FedNow settled 4,997,811 payments worth $274.664 billion in the second quarter of 2026 (54,921 a day), up from 2.7 million payments worth $271.3 billion in the first quarter. There were more than 1,800 live institutions by mid-July 2026 (about 1,600 in January), and the largest payment allowed rose from $500,000 at the July 20, 2023 launch to $1 million in March 2025 and $10 million in November 2025. The library holds only these two quarters of volume, so it cannot show a longer growth trend yet.

graphics.question: Can the President fire a Fed governor?
graphics.answer: Only for cause, and only after notice and a chance to respond. On June 29, 2026 the Supreme Court (5-4) kept Governor Lisa Cook in office, holding that courts can review the 'cause' and that she got no notice or hearing. On October 7 the President set up a committee to try again, with a hearing set for November 5, 2026.

graphics.question: Who regulates insurers: states, Treasury, the Fed or global bodies?
graphics.answer: Mostly the states. Treasury's own 2026 Federal Insurance Office report says the primary regulators of the business of insurance are the 50 states, the District of Columbia and five U.S. territories. Treasury's Federal Insurance Office monitors, advises, represents and administers bounded federal roles; the Financial Stability Oversight Council monitors system risk and can designate a nonbank under section 113; Federal Reserve insurance-group supervision applies only to covered holding companies and designated nonbanks. Global bodies write shared standards, but IAIS adoption is not self-executing state or federal law and does not itself intervene in a group.

graphics.question: How do life insurers' promises turn into private credit and offshore reinsurance?
graphics.answer: Policy and annuity money becomes long-dated liabilities that insurers invest: long promises supply investable general-account liabilities, and insurer asset allocation directs trillions into bonds, mortgages, structured assets and alternatives, including through a private credit and structured-asset channel. The issuing life insurer can then cede liabilities and economics to an asset-intensive reinsurer, secured by a trust, funds withheld or collateral. The NAIC's September 2026 analysis estimated $1.210 trillion of private-credit exposure at year-end 2025 after removing identifiable overlaps. The annual report says total ceded premium increased 32.8% to $580.5 billion and assumed premium increased 48.1% to $272.5 billion. Treasury convened state regulators in 2026 specifically around private credit, offshore reserve movement, RBC, private letter ratings and evolving business models. The hub's limit: Offshore location, reciprocal-jurisdiction status or large ceded reserve does not alone prove weakened security or insolvency.

graphics.question: What changes when an employer moves its pension to an insurer?
graphics.answer: Pension risk transfer changes the legal obligor and protection regime, not merely the asset manager. The chain differs for a buy-in, where the annuity remains a plan asset and the plan continues to owe participants, and a buy-out, where the insurer becomes the direct benefit payer for transferred obligations. PBGC also states that its guarantee ends after plan assets are distributed in a standard termination. The insurer becomes responsible for annuity payments. Any later state guaranty-association protection is state-, residency-, product- and limit-specific.

graphics.question: What happens to your policy if your insurer fails?
graphics.answer: A domestic insurer does not ordinarily enter the same federal bankruptcy process as an industrial company. State insurance law, the domiciliary commissioner and a supervising state court instead control conservation, rehabilitation or liquidation. Liquidation normally triggers the guaranty duty; financial distress alone does not. Coverage, limits, residency and product eligibility are state-law questions. The guaranty system does not make every creditor whole, insure the insurer, or convert failure into a federal bailout.

graphics.question: When does the government pay for insurance losses, and after what trigger?
graphics.answer: It depends on the program, and none pays without its own trigger record. TRIP: federal share after a certified act, insurer deductible and program trigger under statute. NFIP: federal primary flood-insurance program with contractors, reinsurance and borrowing. State catastrophe fund: statutory wholesale reimbursement layer. Guaranty association: limited post-impairment or insolvency protection. PBGC: federal limited guarantee for covered private defined-benefit pensions. An FHLBank advance is a secured liquidity loan from a government-chartered member-owned bank. Program authority and available capacity are not a paid federal claim.

graphics.question: How do catastrophe bonds and reinsurance carry disaster risk?
graphics.answer: Alternative capital adds a funded layer to the reinsurance market. A sponsor transfers a defined risk to a special-purpose vehicle; investors fund collateral and receive a spread; a trigger can reduce principal or release collateral to the sponsor. The original insurer or public program normally remains the direct claimant-facing obligor. A hurricane, flood or earthquake is not itself the security trigger. For ordinary reinsurance the hub's rule is the same: ceded economics do not normally erase the original promise; cession ordinarily does not erase the direct insurer's policyholder obligation or prove that a recovery is due or collectible.

graphics.question: Can a CPA license make you an accredited investor?
graphics.answer: Not yet. On September 30, 2026 the SEC issued Release 33-11446, a notice and request for comment on a possible designation order under Rule 501(a)(10) of Regulation D: a natural person holding an active U.S. CPA license in good standing would qualify personally as an accredited investor, without the income or net-worth tests. It is not a final order; comments are due 60 days after Federal Register publication, and that date was not yet set when the library last checked (October 5, 2026). What a CPA can do today is give a Rule 506(c) written confirmation that another investor is accredited.

graphics.question: What is each Reserve Bank studying in 2026?
graphics.answer: Each Reserve Bank's 2026 conference records cover a different mix of topics. Across the six themes the library tracks, AI adoption and agentic controls is the widest (8 Banks: Boston, Cleveland, Richmond, Minneapolis, Dallas, San Francisco, New York, St. Louis); digital money, clearing and finality has 6; labor flows and regional distribution has 5; data governance and authority has 4; fraud, cyber and operational resilience has 4; power and physical infrastructure has 3 (Dallas, Minneapolis, San Francisco). Philadelphia falls under none of the six: its records are on mortgage transmission and intermediation. A conference topic shows what a Bank is paying attention to, not that it owns the function or has adopted a policy.

graphics.question: What did each House hearing on the Fed set out to change, and who testified?

graphics.question: Which crypto rules are final, which are only proposals, and what does each one actually allow?
graphics.answer: Of the 8 crypto rules, orders and bills the library tracks outside the GENIUS Act, 2 are in effect, 3 are formal proposals, 1 is still at the advance-notice stage, 1 is non-binding staff guidance, and the one market-structure bill, the CLARITY Act, is blocked: the Senate fell short of the 60 votes needed to take it up on September 15, 2026. None of the proposals is final yet.

graphics.question: When you buy into BlackRock's BUIDL fund, send USDC or buy a tokenized share, which company is responsible at each step?
graphics.answer: A different company at almost every step, and the money step is mostly unmapped. In a BUIDL subscription, Securitize Markets, LLC gives eligible investors access, the fund (BlackRock USD Institutional Digital Liquidity Fund Ltd.) issues the shares, Securitize, LLC keeps the share register, and The Bank of New York Mellon must confirm the subscription money first. For USDC, Circle Internet Financial, LLC is the issuer behind each documented step, but a token transfer alone is not a bank payout. For the Coinbase tokenized share, Coinbase Onchain SPV Ltd issues the certificate, Alpaca Securities LLC holds the underlying Apple share, Base carries the token and Onchain Marketplace Limited keeps the Legal Register that decides ownership. Across the three, 10 of 12 money steps are not mapped in the library's evidence.

graphics.question: If you want dollars back from a stablecoin or tokenized fund, who pays you, how fast, and what can stop it?
graphics.answer: It depends on the route, and only the proposed federal rule names a speed. Of the 7 routes the library compares, the issuer or fund pays you back for USDC (Circle, for eligible holders) and USYC (Circle's USDC Teller, whose available liquidity is shown in real time; larger and same-day requests go through support procedures). For BUIDL, the routes are an announced exchange of fund shares for Ripple's RLUSD and trades with whitelisted counterparties on UniswapX, which gives "no assurance of liquidity or pricing." On CHIPS, XRPL and Swift it is participant positions, trading liquidity or banks. What can stop you: holder eligibility, verification, jurisdiction and bank payout timing for USDC; undisclosed bank terms on Swift; withdrawal rules on CHIPS. The Fed's proposal would give issuers no more than 2 business days to redeem after a valid request; it is not final.

graphics.question: What kind of money does each system settle in?
graphics.answer: 30 systems and money instruments, side by side: 5 stablecoin, 10 commercial-bank deposit token, 3 central-bank unit, 1 off-ledger final settlement, 1 carries more than one kind, 10 kind of money not stated in the row. A stablecoin is a claim on its issuer, a deposit token is a claim on one bank, a central-bank unit is a claim on the central bank, and several ledgers only coordinate payments that finally settle somewhere else.

graphics.question: What does each crypto company control, where can it stop a payment, and how does it make money?
graphics.answer: Each controls a different step around the coin, not just the coin. Issuers (Circle, Ripple's Standard Custody, Tether, Paxos, Agora) decide who can mint and redeem, and Tether, Standard Custody and Agora can also freeze tokens; Coinbase and Stripe control listings, accounts and which payments qualify; Anchorage's bank can refuse minting or redemption and freeze or seize tokens under its product terms, while Fireblocks' transfer rules are set by its customers. Issuers earn mostly reserve income (Circle: $652.5 million in the first quarter of 2026, with $405.4 million of distribution and transaction costs); distributors and service firms earn fees.

graphics.question: What does each blockchain network, DeFi protocol and yield product control, where can it stop a payment, and how does it make money?
graphics.answer: Very different amounts. On Ethereum, validators can censor or leave out transactions; on Stellar and Hedera each token's issuer sets its own freeze controls. Aave, Sky and Curve can change settings, caps or fees by governance vote, but Liquity's core design has no way to pause, upgrade or blacklist. Ethena and Ondo control who may mint and redeem; Morpho's governance cannot pause existing markets, while its vault curators choose where lenders' money goes. They earn from network fees, borrowing interest and protocol fees, and Ethena from derivatives funding payments.

graphics.question: At which step of a trade or payment does a crypto company actually replace a bank, broker or registrar?
graphics.answer: At none of them, on the library's walk-through. Across 3 everyday processes (buying a broker-held share, making a dollar payment, subscribing to a fund), 17 steps and 46 seats, the answer to "does it take over?" is No every time. It notes a crypto overlap at 39 seats, meaning "a different claim, a membership, or a software path hanging off the same rail": for example, DTC tokenization can re-represent a participant's entitlement, and Securitize, LLC is the transfer agent for BlackRock's BUIDL fund, a seat it holds "by appointment, not by replacing the fund." In each case the books that count stay with the bank, broker, depository or registrar.

graphics.question: What must a tokenized system prove before it can be trusted with real money, and which systems pass each test?
graphics.answer: No system is shown to pass yet. The library's 14-part readiness test, saved September 22, 2026, asks what a tokenized system must prove, from a legally defined claim to final money and the retirement of old systems, and rates 34 systems on fit only: in its words, "Functional fit is not legal qualification." The strongest candidates are DTC / DTCC tokenization (core on 7), Circle / USDC / CPN / Arc / Tazapay (core on 6) and Securitize (core on 6). No system is a core candidate for test 14, Economics and legacy retirement.

graphics.question: What does the SEC's tokenized-stock exemption allow, and how big can it get?
graphics.answer: SEC Release No. 34-106402, in effect September 17, 2026 through September 17, 2031, lets a qualifying U.S. tokenized securities venue trade tokenized versions of listed U.S. stocks in permissioned automated-market-maker pools on a public, permissionless blockchain without being an 'exchange', and lets firms supplying those pools with their own capital avoid 'dealer' status. Every pair must include a tokenized stock. Size is capped at 75 symbols and 0.25% of prior-month average daily volume for S&P 500, Russell 1000 and qualifying LULD ETPs (Tier 1), and 250 symbols and 2.5% for other eligible NMS stocks (Tier 2). It approves no venue, token or chain; custody, transfer-agent, clearing and settlement law still apply.

graphics.question: Which crypto technologies could fit the SEC's tokenized-stock exemption, and has anyone actually started?
graphics.answer: Plenty could fit, but no one has started under the order. The library reads 20 core systems and 14 added ones against the ten seats an exempt venue needs: 4 are core technical candidates (Ethereum, Stellar, Solana, Algorand), 8 conditional candidates, 5 supporting layers and 3 outside the core design. The only public step so far is Imperium's filing as a prospective liquidity provider on September 28, 2026; it says it has not begun, and no venue notice or launch was found through October 5, 2026.

graphics.question: What does Securitize actually run, and which of its companies holds which license?
graphics.answer: Securitize runs the official ownership record for tokenized funds and stocks, not the money. Through 6 separate companies it acts as an SEC-registered transfer agent, a broker-dealer with a trading system, an investment adviser, a fund administrator and an EU trading-and-settlement operator; each license belongs to that one subsidiary, not to the listed parent.

graphics.question: What has each card network and payment company actually launched with stablecoins?
graphics.answer: Of 32 stablecoin products from card networks and payment companies, 11 are fully live and 10 are live on a limited basis. 5 are pilots and 2 are announced only. In most live products the customer spends stablecoins while the shop is paid in ordinary money.

graphics.question: When a shop "accepts stablecoins," what does the shop actually receive?
graphics.answer: A shop can accept a customer's stablecoin payment and still receive ordinary money. The saved Stripe product credits the merchant in USD, while Shopify defaults to its normal payout currency and lets eligible merchants claim USDC instead. Stablecoin-funded cards also pay shops through ordinary card settlement. Separately, some processors offer stablecoin settlement after shoppers pay normally. The saved records mix live products, limited offerings, pilots and infrastructure; they do not show how most shops are paid.

graphics.question: Who can freeze, burn or block a stablecoin?
graphics.answer: For 18 of the 36 crypto dollars here, the issuer can freeze or block coins, usually for suspected crime or on a court or government order. The GENIUS Act requires payment-stablecoin issuers to be able to do this.

graphics.question: Where does stablecoin interest go if the law bans paying it?
graphics.answer: The GENIUS Act bars an issuer from paying holders interest just for holding the coin. 10 of the 17 issuers here say in their terms that holders get nothing, and 7 don't say. The interest earned on the reserves stays with the issuer, which shares much of it with distributors such as exchanges. Some of those distributors pay their own customers 'rewards', and whether that is allowed is the open question.
graphics.plain_title: Where does stablecoin interest go if the law bans paying it?

graphics.question: Can a stablecoin's issuer change while the coin, wallet and checkout stay the same?
graphics.answer: Yes. Tether moved all of USD₮'s obligations to a new company effective January 27, 2025 without users changing wallets, and SoFi's current SOFID terms already allow a substitute issuer. PayPal moved its wallet customers to PayPal Digital on May 19, 2026, but Paxos stayed PYUSD's issuer. Circle's planned move to a New York issuer, Ripple's reserve bank and Fiserv's FIUSD programs are still plans. In each case the ticker, app and checkout can stay the same while the legal party behind them changes, so the proof is a signed transfer and new terms, not the app.

graphics.question: When a crypto firm collapsed, did its customers get their money back, and how?
graphics.answer: Rarely in full. Of 10 cases the library tracks, customers are being paid back, at least partly, in 3 (Cryptopia liquidation, Mt. Gox civil rehabilitation, FTX Chapter 11 distribution), no payout is confirmed in the library's record for 5, and 1 recovered everything (Wuhan virtual-currency cash-out fraud). How much comes back depends on whether a court treats customer crypto as the customers' own property held in trust or as the failed firm's assets.

graphics.question: Which crypto networks and companies would the Fed's stablecoin rules reach, and how?
graphics.answer: The Federal Reserve Board's two GENIUS Act proposals of September 24, 2026 reach the 20 crypto networks and companies the library maps in four different ways: 2 would face them directly as stablecoin issuers (Ripple / XRPL and Circle / USDC / CPN / Arc / Tazapay); 4 as custody, distribution or payout services (Securitize, Cash legs & tokenized bank money, Coinbase / Base / Tokenize and SWIFT ledger & bank obligations); 12 as technical systems an issuer would run on; and 2 sit outside the direct issuer rules (Bitcoin and DTC / DTCC tokenization). The proposals are not final, and they approve no company, network or token.

graphics.question: When can an investment adviser hold clients' crypto keys itself under the SEC proposal?
graphics.answer: Only as a last resort, and only if the proposal becomes final; the SEC proposed it on October 1, 2026 and no final rule has been issued. For an ordinary advisory client the rule reaches a crypto asset only when it is a fund or security. The adviser may hold the keys itself only when, after a written inquiry, no qualified custodian will hold that particular asset (cost does not count), re-checked at least quarterly, and it must move the asset to a custodian as soon as reasonably practicable once one is available. Only designated supervised people may hold key material, every movement needs at least two of them including a management person, and a technology vendor must not be able to reach the keys or move the assets alone, so a single-employee adviser cannot use the route.

graphics.question: Which states have made gold money or put bitcoin in a state reserve, and when does each take effect?
graphics.answer: Gold, yes; bitcoin, not as money. Florida's gold-and-silver legal-tender law took effect July 1, 2026; in Texas, the law makes gold and silver specie legal tender from September 1, 2026, and the state's electronic gold currency may start no sooner than May 1, 2027. Louisiana (June 11, 2025, with a gold-payment registry added June 23, 2026) and Missouri (July 10, 2025) signed gold legal-tender laws whose start dates are not in the record. For bitcoin the rows show reserves, not money: New Hampshire and Arizona passed reserve laws in May 2025, Texas made the first state purchase on November 20, 2025, and Wisconsin's pension sold its stake. graphics.question: Which accounting jobs can software do, and which still need a person?
graphics.answer: Of the 16 accounting jobs in the library's map, software working from reliable event records can do 6 strongly: identity; authority; settlement; internal control; reconciliation; correction and recovery. Three more are strong once a condition holds: classification, when facts are complete; allocation, for fixed rules; reporting and disclosure, after judgments. graphics.question: Where does the drone beyond-visual-line-of-sight rule (Part 108) stand, and what other drone rules are pending?
graphics.answer: Part 108 is still only a proposal: the FAA and TSA proposed it August 7, 2025, refused more comment time September 29, 2025 and reopened comments on one design question January 28, 2026; the record holds no final rule, although EO 14307 set a 240-day final-rule target ('as appropriate'). The other pending drone rule is the FAA's May 6, 2026 proposal to restrict drones near fixed-site facilities (comments extended to August 5, 2026). 3 items are notices, not rules: Electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing and Advanced Air Mobility Integration Pilot Program — Establishment and Request for Proposals; Implementing Section 927 Waiver Process for Certain Unmanned Aircraft Operations; Unleashing American Drone Dominance (FCC Notice of Inquiry). 2 are final: Integration of Powered-Lift: Pilot Certification and Operations (SFAR); Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports.

graphics.answer: Yes, by DOE's own count. DOE selected 11 projects on August 12, 2025 with a goal of at least three test reactors reaching criticality by July 4, 2026. DOE reported Aalo Atomics' Aalo-X as the pilot's fourth criticality (July 4, 2026, announced July 6, 2026). DOE later called Oklo's Groves (early August) the fifth that summer. The library does not name the first two, and the count is DOE's, not an independent census; criticality is a test milestone, not a commercial license or power delivery.

graphics.question: How do the IMF, the World Bank bodies and the BIS fit together, and where does the Fed connect?
graphics.answer: Treasury speaks for the U.S. at the IMF and the five World Bank Group bodies (IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA, ICSID); the Fed Board is the U.S. member of the BIS. The Fed touches them at 5 points: U.S. policy seat; depositary and fiscal agent; SDR certificate chain; IMF surveillance; BIS membership. None of these gives the IMF or the Bank a say in Fed policy, or the Fed a vote inside them. Treasury's October 14, 2026 statement is a U.S. position, not yet a rule change at any of the institutions.

graphics.question: What does the U.S. pay, and how does it vote, in each international body?
graphics.answer: The U.S. share runs from 49.99% (Organization of American States, 2026 assessed quota) down to 9.09% (ITER, construction sharing baseline). At the UN it pays 22% of the regular budget and 26.1371% of peacekeeping, but still has one Assembly vote. Paying more buys more votes only where votes are weighted by money, at the IMF and World Bank: the U.S. IMF share can block decisions requiring 85% of total voting power; IBRD influence derives from shareholding.

graphics.question: Which international bodies has the U.S. left, and when does each exit take effect?
graphics.answer: The U.S. has fully left 1 body: the Paris Agreement (effective January 27, 2026). Its exit from the World Health Organization is claimed effective January 22, 2026 but disputed: WHO still treated the U.S. as a member in arrears in May 2026. UNESCO exit takes effect December 31, 2026. The parent UN climate treaty (UNFCCC) exit takes effect February 27, 2027. On February 3, 2025 it stopped taking part in the UN Human Rights Council and cut its money to UNRWA, without leaving the UN. For 10 other bodies an exit clause exists but no U.S. notice was found.

graphics.question: How could the U.S. leave each international organization?
graphics.answer: Each of the 27 bodies has its own exit route. Where the founding text names a period, it runs from immediately (Board of Peace) and on receipt of notice (International Monetary Fund) to 90 days (Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons), six months (World Trade Organization, World Intellectual Property Organization), one year (NATO, OECD, International Civil Aviation Organization, International Maritime Organization, International Telecommunication Union) and two years (Organization of American States). For NATO the record adds: 'U.S. domestic statute requires Senate or Congress route'. 3 name a notice route without a period in the record (International Atomic Energy Agency, World Bank Group, ITER). 6 have no simple withdrawal clause (the United Nations Charter has none) and 4 are not memberships the U.S. could leave. 3 exits already carry a date: World Health Organization, UNESCO, Paris Agreement; the WHO exit, stated effective January 22, 2026, is disputed.

graphics.question: Is anything replacing the international bodies the U.S. is leaving?
graphics.answer: Not wholesale: the registry counts 0 wholesale replacements among the 27 bodies (as of October 4, 2026). 17 bodies still do their job with no successor. 4 were left or cut with no successor at all: UN Human Rights Council, UNRWA, UNESCO, Paris Agreement. Only 3 show a changed default route, each for one bounded job: U.S. foreign health aid now goes through the America First Global Health Strategy bilateral network (the WHO's universal functions are retained); WTO appeals for participating non-U.S. Members go through the MPIA; and a U.S. side-by-side tax regime sits inside the OECD. Two pieces of new machinery exist (Artemis Accords, Board of Peace), and Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science is doctrine only. The Board of Peace's Gaza field handoff was incomplete in September 2026.

graphics.question: How does a UN decision get made, paid for and carried out, and who controls each step?
graphics.answer: A General Assembly decision passes through 13 steps, each with its own controller: Member States authorize; a state, organ or the Secretary-General asks for an agenda item; the General Committee filters it; a Main Committee takes the work; sponsors and co-facilitators write the text; the Assembly adopts it (two thirds for budget and other important questions, a simple majority otherwise); then the Fifth Committee and ACABQ decide the money, the Secretary-General carries it out, and auditors and Member States review it. Adoption is not funding, and funding is not delivery.

graphics.question: Japan: if a bank or payment system fails, who takes the loss, in what order?
graphics.answer: On the Japan money map (as of September 15, 2026), a failure moves through 5 separate steps: what sets it off (Ordinary liquidity stress, Operational outage, Systemic failure classification); the private first response (Commercial banks, Japan Securities Clearing Corporation, Zengin System and More Time, FMI default waterfalls); the Bank of Japan's liquidity step (BOJ Policy Board, BOJ current-account balances, BOJ-NET Funds Transfer System, BOJ Article 33 lending, BOJ Article 37 outage lending, BOJ Article 38 special support), which lends against collateral and does not cover a final loss; resolution (Cabinet and Prime Minister, Financial Services Agency, Deposit Insurance Corporation of Japan, TLAC and creditor loss, Deposit protection and transfer); and where the loss finally lands (Fraud compensation and restitution, JPYSC trust stablecoin, Possible retail CBDC, Industry contributions, Conditional fiscal subsidy or guarantee). Public money is a last, conditional step that needs legal and budget approval.

graphics.question: Who runs the City of London and UK public money?
graphics.answer: HM Treasury runs UK public money: it administers the UK Consolidated Fund, the National Loans Fund and the Debt Management Account and owns the Exchange Equalisation Account, the Bank of England and The Royal Mint; the Bank of England (whose capital is held for Treasury, with statutory independence) operates RTGS / CHAPS and acts as Treasury's agent for the Exchange Equalisation Account. Parliament legislates for 'tax, Supply and financial-services law', and the National Audit Office serves it. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each keep their own consolidated fund, answerable to their legislature. The City of London is run by the City of London Corporation, through the Court of Common Council and the Court of Aldermen; it keeps the City Fund, the City's Estate and the City Bridge Foundation separate, and it 'does not set UK tax, regulate UK finance or constitute a state within a state.' It is a different body from the Greater London Authority and the Mayor of London. 'The City' as a financial market is not a legal person: the FCA and the PRA regulate the firms in it.

graphics.question: Who can make law for each part of the UK and its territories?
graphics.answer: The UK Parliament can make law for the whole UK ('Parliamentary sovereignty within the UK constitutional order'). It has handed law-making for devolved matters to three legislatures: the Scottish Parliament (Scotland Act 1998 as amended), Senedd Cymru (Government of Wales Act 2006 as amended) and the Northern Ireland Assembly (Northern Ireland Act 1998 and Agreement settlement). England has no legislature of its own on the map: it is 'predominantly governed through UK institutions, local government and devolved local arrangements'. The 3 Crown Dependencies (Bailiwick of Jersey, Bailiwick of Guernsey, Isle of Man) and 14 British Overseas Territories are not part of the UK. The Crown Dependencies are self-governing under island constitutional law (Jersey answers to its States Assembly, the Isle of Man to Tynwald), linked through the Crown, with the Privy Council handling 'Royal Assent and specified Crown functions'. Each Overseas Territory runs under its own constitution or Orders within the UK constitutional framework, with a Governor or Commissioner; the map does not name each territory's legislature.

graphics.question: Where do Korea's won stablecoin and Han River project stand?
graphics.answer: The won stablecoin still has no law: the Korea country file says that as of October 3, 2026 South Korea had no enacted general public-won stablecoin regime, and that a future won stablecoin's issuer, reserves and redemption rules were unresolved. In the world money record, the Digital Asset Basic Act was introduced June 10, 2025, stalled December 30, 2025 over who may issue the token, the government proposed its own bill April 8, 2026, and on May 12, 2026 it was left off the National Policy Committee's last agenda before recess. The Bank of Korea paused Phase 2 of Project Han River (Hangang), its wholesale CBDC and tokenized-deposit trial with the banks, on June 26, 2025, and relaunched it March 18, 2026 with nine banks, retooled around tokenizing government disbursements; on July 1, 2026 the Bank floated growing it into foreign-bond investment infrastructure; and on July 15, 2026 its Phase II designation was expanded, with Kyongnam and iM Bank newly designated. The country file treats Hangang tokens as commercial-bank deposit claims in a controlled pilot; no public-won issuer or production wholesale CBDC was established.

graphics.question: Who insures exporters and overseas investors against nonpayment or seizure?
graphics.answer: Four kinds of risk bearer, in the study's map. For exporters: a private trade-credit insurer, which insures commercial or political nonpayment within limits and conditions, and EXIM export-credit insurance, which covers a stated share of eligible foreign-receivable nonpayment. For overseas investors: DFC political-risk insurance, which covers selected inconvertibility, expropriation, violence and contract risks, and the World Bank Group's MIGA guarantee and risk-sharing facility, which covers qualifying cross-border financing and may share first loss with donor or IDA resources. Export-credit insurance protects an exporter or lender against defined nonpayment. Political-risk insurance protects a qualifying investment or financing against named government or conflict risks. Neither makes the buyer's debt disappear, guarantees a country's currency value, covers physical cargo loss by default, or authorizes a transaction prohibited by sanctions.

graphics.question: Which foreign places matter for U.S. insurance, and how is each recognized under U.S. rules?
graphics.answer: Seven places in the study's jurisdiction table: the European Union, the United Kingdom, the Bermuda, the Cayman Islands, the Japan, the Switzerland and the United States itself. The NAIC list available at the cutoff identifies EU member states and the UK through covered agreements; Bermuda, Japan and Switzerland are listed as qualified-jurisdiction reciprocal jurisdictions. Bermuda's listing is limited to named commercial and long-term insurer classes. Cayman is not listed in that document. The U.S.–EU agreement entered into force on April 4, 2018; the U.S.–UK agreement entered into force on December 31, 2020. In 2026 Treasury's Federal Insurance Office signed a memorandum with Bermuda's regulator and a cooperation statement with Cayman's; they are not covered agreements, reciprocal-jurisdiction designations, treaty approvals, licences or guarantees.

graphics.question: The rules: who is allowed to do what, and is it law yet?
graphics.answer: This page reads every rule the library holds on U.S. crypto in one walk: the GENIUS Act (enacted July 18, 2025) and its 28 dated steps, 14 of them proposals not yet final; the 8 other crypto rules, orders and bills and where each stands; the Crypto Hub's nine-step legal process walk with its 7 worked cases and qualification records; the SEC's custody proposal provision by provision (36 provisions, all 760 pages and 342 comment questions); the CFTC's 30-provision baseline; the SEC's Innovation Exemption (12 conditions, 15 clocks); the Federal Reserve Board's two GENIUS proposals; and 9 other jurisdictions' laws. A proposal grants no permission to anyone until it is final.
graphics.plain_title: Crypto laws and proposed rules

graphics.question: The money: what is the dollar on the chain, who owes it, and what backs it?
graphics.answer: This page reads every crypto dollar the library tracks: 36 coins and tokens (17 of them payment stablecoins or candidates), each with its exact issuing company, legal route, reserves and who holds them, attestation, redemption terms, size, freeze power (33 can freeze) and yield; then the July card decks that first mapped issuers, DeFi dollars, company control and GENIUS events; the Crypto Hub's 54 cash-leg nodes, which separate a stablecoin from a bank deposit and from central-bank money; and the dated filings and central-bank digital money moves. Who owes the dollar is always a named legal entity, not a brand or a chain.
graphics.plain_title: Crypto dollars: issuers, backing and holders’ rights

graphics.question: The records: which record controls title, and what gets booked
graphics.answer: This page follows the record, not the token: who books what, and whose record decides who owns it. It opens with the 3 process walks of how a trade, a payment and a fund subscription work today, and the debit-and-credit entries each party books at every step; then the steps-and-rights walks and transaction maps; the 17 asset traces (USDC from mint to redemption, BUIDL and others); the 7 accounting layers; the current U.S. stack; Securitize's 4 record models; DTC's records; the SEC transfer agent proposal; and 61 dated tokenization and clearing filings. A token, a chain or a software vendor books nothing by itself; only an entity whose own books hold the asset or the claim does.
graphics.plain_title: Ownership records and accounting entries

graphics.question: The operators: which companies and networks run it, and how far along is each?
graphics.answer: This page reads every operator the library tracks and how far along each one is, in one status vocabulary: 16 banks and asset managers across seven capabilities with where the proof stops, 32 card and processor products, 12 market systems, the money-machine seats; the bank transition, corporate stack and stack expansion comparisons; the Crypto Hub's 23 families with all 302 nodes and 372 connections; the field guide, the build-out ledger and the 112 vetted October 19 updates; and the 220 named actors and every placement. Announced is not live, and a partnership is not control.
graphics.plain_title: Companies and payment networks

graphics.question: The access: who may touch the Fed, and who holds a charter or license?
graphics.answer: This page reads every gate between crypto firms and the dollar system: the 36 institutions in the Fed-account and bank-charter queue, firm by firm (2 with a full master account, 1 with a limited account, 1 waiting, 1 in court); the 4 account types and what each allows; the queue counts; the 59-entry dated charter record; the legal routes map (26 jobs, 52 routes, 57 firms and public bodies); the 14 transition gates; the court cases on Fed accounts and on removing a Fed governor; and every legal placement. A charter and a Fed account are separate decisions by different agencies.
graphics.plain_title: Bank charters and Federal Reserve accounts

graphics.question: The settlement: where does the cash finally settle, and in what kind of money?
graphics.answer: In most of what the library holds, the cash still settles in money that already existed. Swift's ledger coordinates commitments among 17 listed banks, 8 of which have a completed pairing located; final settlement happens afterwards through existing payment systems. Of the 12 market systems, 1 settles in central-bank money by the master's own description (Sterling Fnality Payment System), 4 move banks' own tokenized deposits, and for 7 the master does not say. Who finances the interval before settlement: banks validated funding and managed the interval before external settlement. Customer availability can precede bank cash receipt.
graphics.plain_title: How payments settle

graphics.question: Failure and remedy: when it breaks, who can freeze, who pays, who decides?
graphics.answer: For 18 of the 36 crypto dollars the library tracks, the issuer can freeze or block coins; for 15 the terms read do not say. When a firm collapsed, customers were being paid back at least partly in 3 of the 10 cases on the International Crypto Map, and courts decided whether customer crypto was the customer's property or the estate's. The 7 programmable-payment failures were corrected by forks, freezes or restitution, not one rule. 37 of 41 U.S. jurisdictions in the register have enacted UCC Article 12, the law on who owns a controllable electronic record.
graphics.plain_title: Failures, losses and customers’ rights

graphics.question: The world: how do the other jurisdictions do it?
graphics.answer: The International Crypto Map reads 22 jurisdictions on 13 dimensions each, from who has authority to who bears a loss; 191 of the 286 cells are researched, 85 partial and 10 still open. 7 of its 14 issuer records are live under a local license, 15 cross-border routes were reviewed and none is yet a recurring end-to-end corridor in the record, and most systems still finish in an existing bank or central-bank record.
